title: Categoriae Decem Ex Aristotele Decerpatae
author: Augustine

passages.original: Is igitur nos docuit ex octo his, quas grammatici partes orationis vocant, cam solam recte appellari orationis partem, quæ indicaret aliquid, vocabuloque signaret. Itaque solas orationis partes, auctore Aristotele, nomen et vorbum debemus accipere: cæteras vero ex his fieri, ci compagines orationis potius, quam partes ejus debere nominari. Nomen namque personam demonstrat, verbum quid quisque faciat patiaturve.
passages.english: He, then, taught us that of these eight, which the grammarians call the parts of speech, that one alone is rightly called a part of speech which indicates something and marks it with a word. Therefore, on Aristotle's authority, we ought to take only the noun and the verb as parts of speech, and [hold] that the others are formed from these and ought to be called the joints of speech rather than its parts. For the noun points out the person, the verb what each one does or undergoes.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: 'cam' for 'eam', 'vorbum' for 'verbum', 'ci' for 'et'.

passages.original: cumdc picto idem non possis dicere, necessario inveniuntur esse disparia. Rcgulariler autem accipere debemus, omne nomen licet proprium, quod possit esse commune cum cæteris, homonymon vocari; ut Cicero, nun unus, sed plurcs. Sed si omisso nomine signis potius demonstrare velis quis sit ille Cicero, quis alius, quis tertius ; alia dc aho signa narranda sunt, ut attium crassum dicas, alium tenuem;
passages.english: [since you] cannot say the same of the painted one, they are necessarily found to be dissimilar. As a rule, moreover, we ought to understand that every noun, even a proper one, which can be shared with others, is called homonymous; as Cicero [is] not one but many. But if, leaving aside the name, you wish rather to show by signs who that Cicero is, who another, who a third, different signs must be stated for each, so that you call one stout, another thin;
passages.notes: Opening 'cumdc picto' read as 'cum de picto'; 'attium' read as 'alium', 'aho' as 'alio'.

passages.original: Synonyma vero sunt, res quæ et nomine et sui interpretatione junguntur, ut cat animal: id enim de homine, et equo, et de fera, ct de avibus dici potest. Animal est quod cibum capiat, quod mortale sit, quod sensu moveatur. Nunc ad eas res, quæ singulæ multis nominibus signari solent, vcniamus. Quanqnam hanc partem Aristoteles, ut snperius dicunt est, prætermiserit, ideirco quod de his quæ significantur, non de his quæ significant, disserendum putavit. In his autem non rerum, sed nominum vertitur quæstio. Hæc divisa sunt similiter in partes duas, ct alia πολυώνυμα, alia έτερὠνυμα.
passages.english: Synonyms, on the other hand, are things which are joined both by name and by their definition, as 'animal': for this can be said of a man, a horse, a wild beast and birds. An animal is that which takes food, which is mortal, which is moved by sense. Now let us come to those things which individually are usually marked by many names. Aristotle, as was said above, passed over this part, because he thought one should discuss the things that are signified, not those that signify. In these, however, the question turns not on things but on names. These are likewise divided into two parts, and some are [called] *polyōnyma* (polyonyms), others *heterōnyma* (heteronyms).

passages.original: Ergo quanquam separatim postea ea quæ sunt, definitarus sit; mixtam tamen de tribus disputationem debemus accipere. Nam de perceptis qui loquitur, et originem rerum trahit, et præsidia orationis implorat Superfluam igitur quæstionem movet, qui dicit scrutan oportere cur Aristoteles in principto suo homonyma lege vel dixcrit, vel detoxerit, si de his qua* percipiuntur fuerat tractaturus, cum liqueat non posse dici aliquid, nisi quod perceptum fuerit, nec percipi aliquid posse, nisi res fuerit de qua imago intuendo capiatur.
passages.english: So although he will afterwards define separately the things that are, we must nevertheless take the discussion as a mixed one concerning the three. For one who speaks of things perceived both draws on the origin of things and calls on the aid of speech. He therefore raises a superfluous question who says that one must inquire why Aristotle at his beginning either spoke of homonyms or [the text is unclear], if he was going to treat of the things that are perceived; since it is clear that nothing can be said except what has been perceived, and nothing can be perceived unless there is a thing from which an image is taken by looking at it.
passages.notes: 'lege vel dixcrit, vel detoxerit' is corrupt; perhaps 'legem vel dixerit vel detexerit' ('stated or disclosed the rule')—uncertain.

passages.original: In subjecto autem nullo est, cum ipse sit usia, quam superius diximus in nullo unquam subjacenti esse; quippe cum sit cæteris ipsa subjecta. Alia vero nec in subjecto sunt, nec de subjecto significantur, ut est Cicero; nec in subjecto est, quia usia est; nec de subjecto aliquo significatur, siquidem cum a se ortum vocabulum teneat, neque intelligi possit aliunde. Dicta sunt duo qua: ad usian pertinent, quo pacto significentur, quorum superius ϰοινὸν, id est commune;
passages.english: But it is in no subject, since it is itself *ousia* (substance), which we said above is never in anything underlying; inasmuch as it is itself the subject for the rest. Others, again, are neither in a subject nor signified of a subject, as is Cicero: he is not in a subject, because he is *ousia*; nor is he signified of any subject, since he holds a name arising from himself and cannot be understood from elsewhere. Two things pertaining to *ousia* have been stated, [namely] how they are signified: of which the higher is called *koinon*, that is, common;

passages.original: Dehinc nos Aristoteles docet. et illa quæ de subjecto significantur, qua ratione noscamus. In hisautcm speciale illud est, quod eadem in ipso subjecto inveniuntur, quæ sunt in eo quod de subjecto significatur: ut enim animal de subjecto significatur, homine vel equo, sic et homode subjecto aliquo homine significetur necesse est: Cicero autem et homo est et animal.
passages.english: Next Aristotle teaches us by what reasoning we may recognize also those things which are signified of a subject. In these the special point is that the same things are found in the subject itself which are in what is signified of the subject: for just as 'animal' is signified of a subject, man or horse, so also 'man' must be signified of a subject, some individual man; and Cicero is both a man and an animal.

passages.original: Neque cnim jam intelligitur vel quid imperativum sit, vcl quid optativum, vcl quid interiogativum, vel quid vocativum, nisi accesserit genus ὰποϕαντιϰὸν, id est pronuntiativum, quod habeat in se quamdam confirmandi sententiam, quae aliquid.aut addat aut dcmat: quod Aristoteles ϰατάϕασιν et ἀποϕασιν dixit, ut est, coelum hoc volubile est, coelum hoc nonest volubile. Ipsum denique pronuntiativum, quod diximus ὰποϕαντιϰὀν, aut falsum ast aut verum. Quamobrem omissis illis quatuor quae magis ad grammaticos vel oratores pertinent, hujus apophantiei, quod ad philosophos attingit, Aristoteles habuit mentionem.
passages.english: For neither the imperative, nor the optative, nor the interrogative, nor the vocative is yet understood unless there is added the *apophantikon* kind, that is, the declarative, which contains in itself a certain affirming sense that either adds or removes something: which Aristotle called *kataphasis* and *apophasis* (affirmation and negation), as: 'this heaven rotates', 'this heaven does not rotate'. Finally, the declarative itself, which we called *apophantikon*, is either false or true. Therefore, leaving aside those four, which belong rather to grammarians or orators, Aristotle made mention of this apophantic [kind], which concerns philosophers.

passages.original: Ilas crgo secundas substantias nominari dicit, propterea quod illa sii potior, quæ ncque in subjecto est, neque de subjecto prædicatur. Secundæ autem substantiæ idcirco dictæ sunt genus et species, quod solæ indicent primam. Ut si quis nolit vel nesciat dicere Socratem, dicat auimal vel hominem, id est genus vel speciem, bis vcro dictis quid sit Socrates agnoscitur; aliud autem si dicut, vel currit, vel ambulat, nibil possit agnosci. Manifestum est autem ea quæ de subjecto significantur, cum iis, quæ subjectum sunt, ct nomen et rationem nominis habere communem;
passages.english: He says, therefore, that these are named secondary substances, because that one is superior which is neither in a subject nor predicated of a subject. And genus and species are called secondary substances for this reason, that they alone indicate the primary one. So that if someone does not wish, or does not know how, to say "Socrates", he may say "animal" or "man", that is, the genus or the species, and when these are said, what Socrates is is recognised; but if he says something else, such as "runs" or "walks", nothing could be recognised. And it is clear that those things which are signified of a subject have in common with those which are the subject both the name and the definition of the name;
passages.notes: Several scanning errors corrected silently (e.g. Ilas crgo = Illas ergo, sii = sit, auimal = animal, bis vcro = his vero, dicut = dicat, nibil = nihil). "Rationem nominis" rendered "definition of the name" (Aristotle's logos).

passages.original: Considerata ergo definitione hujus categoriae, poterit etiam confusionis ex similitudine exortæ discretio reperiri. Eodem pacto possumus hanc categoriam et ab oppositornm similitudine separare. Nam et opposita άντιϰείμενα. Aristoteles vocat, quamdam hujus categoriæ sirnililudinem reddunt: siquidem calidum et frigidum videntur sibi oppositionis societate conjuncta : sed calidum non frigidi calidum, sed frigido oppositum dicimus; et justum non injusti justum, sed injusto contrarium nominamus.
passages.english: So when the definition of this category has been considered, a way of distinguishing the confusion arising from similarity can also be found. In the same way we can separate this category from the similarity of opposites. For opposites too, which Aristotle calls *antikeimena*, present a certain similarity to this category: hot and cold, indeed, seem joined to one another by the bond of opposition; but we do not call hot the hot of the cold, but opposed to the cold; and we do not call just the just of the unjust, but contrary to the unjust.

passages.original: in jaccre, pronus autsupinus jacet; in habere, decenter armatus. Erit igitur non parvæ prudentiæ, qualitatem cum cereris pene confusam, mentis vivacitate secernere. Hujus sunt species numero quatuor, quas Aristoteles pro generibus posuit, scilicet propterea quia et ipsæ singulæ habent species suas. Id vero cum acciderit, subalterna nominantur, quæ Græci ύπάλληλα vocaverunt. Ergo primum genus est habitus ct affectio : secundum, potentia naturalis : tertium, passivæ qualitates sive passions : quartum, formæ ac figuræ.
passages.english: in lying, he lies face down or face up; in having, handsomely armed. It will therefore take no small prudence to separate by sharpness of mind quality, which is almost blended with the others. Its species are four in number, which Aristotle set down as genera, namely because each of them also has its own species. When this happens, they are called subaltern, which the Greeks called *hypallēla*. So the first genus is habit and disposition; the second, natural capacity; the third, passive qualities or affections; the fourth, forms and shapes.

passages.original: Sequitur ut de jacere dicamus, sive de situ, ut quidam putant: quæ categoria in ad aliquid relatis jam videtur esse tractata. Siquidem quod jacet, posttum jacet : positum vero positionis est, et positio positi. Qua de causa, ut ipse quoque Aristoteles, quem sequimur, fecit, ad alia transeamus.
passages.english: It follows that we speak of lying, or of position, as some think: a category which seems already to have been treated among relatives. For what lies, lies placed; and the placed is [placed] by a position, and position is of the placed. For this reason, as Aristotle himself, whom we follow, also did, let us pass on to other matters.

passages.original: Nee affirmatio et negatio idem est, quod sunt sub affirmatione negationeque cadentia. Affirmatio enim sive negatio, est verbum confirmans aliquid aut negans; alia vero sunt, quæ sub his inveniuntur, ut est, Socratesdisserit, Socrates non disserit. Similitcr tamen omnia sibi habentur opposita. Aliquoties autem mala malis opponuntur, quoties contrariorum media bona sunt, ut est indigentia et redundantia, quae Cræci ἒνδειαν ϰαὶ ὑπερολὴν vocant.
passages.english: Nor are affirmation and negation the same as the things that fall under affirmation and negation. For an affirmation or negation is a statement affirming or denying something; but the things found under them are different, as in "Socrates is discoursing", "Socrates is not discoursing". Yet all these are likewise held to be opposed to one another. Sometimes, moreover, evils are opposed to evils, whenever the means between contraries are good, as with deficiency and excess, which the Greeks call endeia and hyperbolē.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected (Nee = Nec, Cræci = Graeci). The Greek ὑπερολὴν is a misprint for ὑπερβολήν (excess). "Verbum" taken in the sense of "statement".
